name: Bilal Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Bilal, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign for anything. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. This is a made-up study built around people like you, and there are no right answers. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Monday to Wednesday are packed: circuits, calculus and an intro to programming in Python. Thursday afternoons I'm in the robotics society workshop, where six of us are building a line-following cart that keeps driving into the wall. On weekends I take the train home, about an hour, and my little brother Idris (he's 14) makes me explain whatever I learned. I share a flat with three guys from my course and we cook in turns, badly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What drew you to electrical engineering?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My mum's a pharmacist and my dad manages a bus depot, so I grew up around systems that have to run on time. I liked that engineering is about making real things work. I had top grades, my parents cover fees and rent, and I'm not carrying any debt. I use the AI chatbot now and then when a Python error confuses me, but I always check it against the textbook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first of five pictures. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get back to normal. I use the chatbot for debugging and it helps about as much as a decent tutor, so I can believe it stays a modest tool. I'd tell my flatmates not to bet their whole degree on predictions from people who sell software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel pretty settled. Electrical engineering has a steady demand for people who can design and test things, and nothing in this picture changes that. I'd still worry a little about wages for juniors, since firms use any excuse to hold pay down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: finish the cart project, apply for a summer internship at a power company, and keep using the chatbot only for small things. I'd also join the course union branch, since I believe in people having a say at work. And I'd keep my Saturday job idea on hold, because my parents want me to study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels comfortable, almost too comfortable. I'd enjoy it while it lasted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said junior wages might be held down. Is that something you've seen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Karim graduated last year in logistics and was offered a contract that paid less than his student job. His manager said it was the market. I'd like to see rules on minimum pay for graduate roles, because nobody's going to hand that over for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what does a summer internship mean to you at this stage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly proof that I can work in a team. A first-year doesn't know much, but a power company lets you shadow engineers on a substation. I'd ask them lots of questions, then decide if I like fieldwork or the lab side more.

say: I'd tell flatmates not to bet their degree on predictions from **software sellers**.
I'd say AI is a decent **tutor**, not a revolution.
think: I feel **settled**, since electrical engineers who design and test things stay in demand.
I worry a little that junior **wages** get held down anyway.
do: Finish the robot **cart** and apply for a summer internship at a power company.
Use the chatbot only for **small** debugging jobs.
Join the course union branch to have a **say** at work.
S0.quote: I'd like to see rules on minimum pay for graduate roles, because nobody's going to hand that over for free.
fieldNote: Steady and practical; trusts the textbook over the chatbot and sees AI as a **tutor**.
His one concern in a quiet world is pay, drawn from his cousin Karim's contract.
Family money gives him room, so mood is calm without being smug.

steps.text: Apply for a summer internship at a regional power company
Join the course union branch and attend monthly meetings
Use the chatbot only to debug small Python errors

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the point where a degree has to prove itself. Software taking over checking, planning and coding means some junior roles shrink, and I'd say we should plan for that with training support and clear rules, not just hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel more pressure. Some of what we learn in first-year programming is exactly what the card says gets automated. But electrical work touches hardware, power and safety, and robots are slower to arrive there, so I'd feel like I picked a slightly safer corner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put more of my time into the hardware side: power electronics, control systems and the robotics society. I'd pick a summer placement where I'm testing equipment, not writing reports. And I'd use the AI tools more regularly now, since I'm competing with people who do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a rising tide. I can swim, I just don't want to be caught in the shallow end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks in your own course do you think software would take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The routine code, the unit tests, probably the documentation. Honestly, the parts I do when I'm tired. What it can't do easily is plug in a board, find that a wire's loose and figure out why a motor is hot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My flatmate Marek, who's doing pure software engineering. He wants a job at a bank writing internal tools, which is exactly what firms would hand to software first. I'd tell him to add something with hardware or data, and I'd mean it kindly.

say: I'd say a degree has to prove itself, and we need **training support** and clear rules.
I'd say hoping is not a **plan**.
think: I feel **pressure**, because first-year programming is what gets automated.
I picked a slightly safer corner in **hardware** and power.
do: Move my time toward **power electronics** and control systems.
Pick a summer placement **testing** equipment rather than writing reports.
Use AI tools **regularly**, because rivals already do.
feel: Like a rising **tide**: I can swim, but not in the shallow end.
S1.quote: What it can't do easily is plug in a board, find that a wire's loose and figure out why a motor is hot.
fieldNote: Judges exposure well: sees which parts of his own course are routine and which need a **hand** in the world.
Worries aloud about his flatmate Marek, a pure software student aiming at bank tools.
Steady adaptability shows: he uses AI more only because rivals do.

steps.text: Choose power electronics and control systems as next term's options
Book a summer placement testing equipment at a power firm
Use an AI assistant for unit tests and documentation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that two years is too short for anyone to cope without help, and governments need to act now: income support, retraining, public jobs if necessary. I'd say it on the union page and to my parents' friends at dinner who think this is hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be scared and trying to hide it. I'd be in second year when thinking AI can do almost anything a person can, and I wouldn't know what a degree is worth. The hands-on side lasts until about 2031, which buys me a little, but I'd be graduating around then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the course and shift to the most physical parts: lab work, installation, anything with my hands. I'd ask my dad's depot about their electric bus charging work, because that kind of equipment needs engineers on site. I'd also open a savings account in my own name with my first summer wages, small as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the ground is moving and nobody's saying where to stand. I'd be short with my mum on the phone, and she'd notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your parents' money really protect you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents' money protects me from the next two years, not the twenty after. If everyone's job is shaken, my mum's pharmacy and my dad's depot are shaken too. So I'd feel the pressure at home even if my own fees are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do first in the week this card became real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call my brother Idris (he's 14) and my parents together, and say we should talk about money plans and what he should study. Then I'd go to the robotics society and ask the older students what they're doing.

say: I'd say two years is too short and we need **income support** and public jobs.
I'd tell sceptical family friends this is **not** hype.
think: I'd be **scared** and hide it, with no idea what a degree is worth.
The hands-on side lasts until about **2031**, which buys me a little.
do: Shift toward lab work, **installation** and other physical engineering.
Ask my dad's depot about **electric bus** charging jobs.
Open a **savings** account with my first summer wages.
feel: Like the **ground** is moving and nobody says where to stand.
S2.quote: My parents' money protects me from the next two years, not the twenty after.
fieldNote: He sees that family wealth is **tied** to the same economy: his mother's pharmacy and father's depot are exposed too.
Hides fear in public and admits it privately, a clear gap between say and think.
First move is to talk with family and robotics society peers, a collective instinct.

steps.text: Shift next term's options toward lab and installation work
Ask the bus depot about charging-equipment work for summers
Open a savings account and pay in half of each summer wage
Talk through money plans with parents and younger brother

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to do something sensible. I'd say we should use the time for retraining schemes and to rewrite what universities teach, and I'd ask the course leaders what they plan to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel moderately worried. I'd graduate in about three years, and graduate hiring would be rough, but I'd have time to add skills that aren't easily copied. The robots arrive around 2034, so hands-on work gives me about three more years than a pure desk job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and look for a master's in control or robotics. I'd get a placement every summer so I'm known to a couple of firms. I'd practise with AI tools properly, not just for debugging, because by then they're part of the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long hill. Tiring, but I can see the top and I can plan the climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change how you talk to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. With two years I'd be pushing them to change plans at once. With five, I can have calm conversations about my brother's choices and about my mum selling the pharmacy lease later if she wants. It's less dramatic and more useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently from the two-year picture, concretely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the master's instead of rushing to find any paid job. I'd save slowly, not sell anything fast. Having time means I can be steady, and steady is how I'd describe myself anyway.

say: I'd say five years is enough for **retraining schemes** and a rewrite of what universities teach.
I'd ask course leaders what they plan to **change**.
think: I feel **moderately** worried about graduate hiring in about three years.
Hands-on engineering gives me roughly three more years than a **desk** job.
do: Apply for a **master's** in control or robotics after the degree.
Get a **placement** every summer so firms know me.
Practise with AI tools **properly**, since they'll be part of the job.
feel: Like a long **hill**: tiring, but I can plan the climb.
S3.quote: Having time means I can be steady, and steady is how I'd describe myself anyway.
fieldNote: The warning time turns **panic** into planning; he talks calmly about his parents and brother.
Chooses further study over rushing into any paid job, which his family money allows.
Consistent with his steady profile: plans in stages rather than leaps.

steps.text: Apply for a master's in control systems or robotics
Take a placement every summer at a different engineering firm
Practise with AI design and testing tools beyond debugging

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if people use it, and a waste if they don't. I'd say we should start training programmes and not leave the next generation to work it out alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fairly relaxed about my own path. Ten years takes me through the degree and into a first job, and by 2039 I'd have built experience that machines will find hard to copy. The thing I'd keep in mind is that nobody really knows the date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am: finish the degree, get a graduate role in power or robotics, and keep learning the new tools as they come. I'd save a share of my first salary each month. And I'd keep taking part in the union and the robotics society, because those people are my network.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels almost normal. I'd keep it in the back of my mind like a long school project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the first sign for you that things were moving faster than predicted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If graduate engineering roles started disappearing in my brother's year, not just in mine. Or if my dad's depot stopped hiring mechanics and bought a charging robot instead. Those are the ordinary things I'd watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you talk to your brother Idris differently in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd tell Idris to study something he enjoys and to learn how to learn. With ten years, there's no point scaring a fourteen-year-old. I'd say to him: be curious, make things, and don't let anyone sell you a panic.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** if people use it.
I'd say the next generation shouldn't have to **work it out** alone.
think: I feel fairly **relaxed**, since ten years takes me into a first job with experience.
I remind myself **nobody** knows the date.
do: Finish the degree and get a graduate role in **power** or robotics.
Save a share of my first **salary** each month.
Stay in the **union** and robotics society as my network.
feel: Almost **normal**, like a long school project in the back of my mind.
S4.quote: With ten years, there's no point scaring a fourteen-year-old.
fieldNote: The decade lets him be **generous** with his younger brother; he plans to keep Idris curious, not frightened.
Names concrete early signs: graduate roles vanishing, the depot buying a charging robot.
Calm follows from time plus family money, and he says the date is unknowable.

steps.text: Finish the degree and target a graduate role in power or robotics
Put aside a fixed share of the first salary monthly
Stay active in the union and robotics society

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture. It lands on my family and my brother's future all at once, and nobody's ready. What would help is clear public support in advance, like retraining you can start without losing income, and honest warnings from universities about which courses are exposed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'd like people to remember not everybody has parents who can pay. My answers are easy because I'm covered. I'd want the plans to work for someone whose family isn't.

headlineQuote: My answers are easy because I'm covered. I'd want the plans to work for someone whose family isn't.
portrait: Bilal is an 18-year-old **electrical engineering** student with top grades, whose parents cover everything and who has no debt.
He uses the chatbot occasionally, checks it against the textbook, and has a sensible, steady way of changing plans.
He leans left and joins the **course union**, wanting rules on graduate pay and public support.
He leans toward hardware and power work, judging it safer than pure software, and worries about his flatmate Marek.
His mood stays calm or uneasy except in the **two-year** picture, where he turns anxious.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture hits his family and his brother's future all at once.
whatWouldHelp: Public support in advance, such as **retraining** without lost income, and honest university warnings about exposed courses.
